title: Atlas and Ledger
premise: In the winter of 1917, Juniper Thornbury, a battlefield nurse near a contested river crossing, secretly records in her ledger the names of the dead and disappeared that official reports erase. When orders come to evacuate and the season's last bridge closes, she is trapped on the wrong side with her ledger, a wounded officer who knows too much, and a victors' historical commission arriving with the thaw. To get the truth on the record before the ice breaks, Juniper must smuggle her names across the river and choose between her own survival and testimony that could destroy the men who wrote the omissions. She crosses as the ice shatters, delivering the ledger to a reluctant archivist, though not everyone she loves makes it out.
about_author: Jude Dunmore is the pen name of a former hospital archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed letters from the First World War. They write from a farmhouse where the river still floods every spring.

chapters.title: What the Forms Leave Out
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. In a dressing station by the river, Juniper begins recording names the casualty reports omit — orderlies, deserters, local women. Her colleague Marta warns her that paper is dangerous. The emotional beat is quiet defiance: the ledger becomes both comfort and threat.

chapters.title: The Officer Who Counted Twice
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Captain Ellery Voss arrives wounded, and Juniper recognizes his signature on reports that erased forty men from a retreat he survived. He begs her to burn nothing yet says nothing outright. The beat is uneasy intimacy built on mutual knowledge of guilt.

chapters.title: Orders for the Season
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Evacuation orders arrive; the bridge will close at first frost. Command demands the ward's paperwork be 'simplified' before transfer. Juniper copies her ledger into duplicate pages hidden in bandage wrappers. The beat is mounting dread beneath bureaucratic calm.

chapters.title: Frost on the Wire
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. Marta reveals she once kept her own list and lost a brother to an omission; she agrees to help carry the ledger out. A raid scatters the ward, and one page goes missing. The beat is fragile alliance forged through shared grief.

chapters.title: The Bridge Closes
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The bridge shuts early after a shell damages its span; Juniper, Voss, and Marta are stranded with the wounded. Voss confesses he signed the false report under threat. The beat is claustrophobia turning to resolve: they will go over the ice if they must.

chapters.title: The Commission Arrives
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The victors' historical commission reaches the far bank, interviewing survivors and collecting 'verified' accounts. An officer offers Juniper safe passage in exchange for her silence about the retreat. The beat is temptation sharpened into moral crisis.

chapters.title: Names in the Bandages
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. The commission searches the ward for 'unauthorized documents.' Marta misdirects them while Juniper sews ledger pages into a dead soldier's effects. Voss decides to testify, knowing it means arrest. The beat is terror transmuted into purpose.

chapters.title: Over the Ice
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Under cover of a fog, the three cross the frozen river carrying the wounded and the ledger. The ice groans; Marta falls through saving a stretcher case and drowns with half the duplicate pages. The beat is devastating cost — survival purchased with loss.

chapters.title: The Historians' Table
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. On the far bank, Juniper confronts the commission, presenting the surviving ledger alongside Voss's signed confession. The archivist hesitates, then enters the names into the record over an officer's objection. The beat is hard-won vindication shadowed by everything omitted even now.

chapters.title: What the River Keeps
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV, years later. Juniper visits the archive where the ledger rests beside the official history that now contradicts it. She adds Marta's name in the margin. The beat is bittersweet resolution: memory preserved imperfectly, identity carried in what survives.
